title: How Britain Lost America: The American Revolution From Both Sides
sources: Our American Revolution, The Price of Peace: https://ouramericanrevolution.org/index.cfm/page/view/m0031
The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, William Franklin: https://franklinpapers.org/bio?id=25
History of Parliament, Lord North and Yorktown: https://historyofparliament.com/2013/09/04/lord-north-and-yorktown/
The Canadian Encyclopedia, Treaty of Paris 1783: https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/treaty-of-paris-1783
American Battlefield Trust, Petitioning the King and Parliament: https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/petitioning-king-and-parliament

beats.say: Benjamin Franklin helped tear America away from the British Empire. His own son fought just as hard to keep it British.
In 1763, Britain had just won the biggest war the world had ever seen. It took Canada from France. It took Florida from Spain. It was the most powerful empire on Earth.
Twenty years later, it had lost almost all of America.
This is the American Revolution. The Revolutionary War, 1775 to 1783. But you've probably only ever heard one side of it. Today, you get both.
Let's start in London, because this story starts with a bill.
Britain had just won the Seven Years' War. In North America, that meant throwing France out of Canada. Wonderful news. Bells, fireworks, songs about how wonderful Britain was.
Then somebody opened the accounts.

talk.text: A hundred and thirty-two million, sir.

beats.say: The national debt had nearly doubled, to about one hundred and thirty two million pounds. Back home, landowners were already handing a quarter of their income to the government.

rows: Yearly cost of 7,500 soldiers in America (pounds)
card.note: Our American Revolution, The Price of Peace

beats.say: And now Britain had a huge new empire to guard. Keeping seven and a half thousand soldiers in America would cost about two hundred and twenty five thousand pounds a year.
That's thirty pounds a year, for every single soldier.
So London looked across the Atlantic at its thirteen colonies, and thought something that seemed perfectly reasonable in London.

talk.text: We just saved you from France. Now pay up.
Happy to discuss it. Who do we vote for?

beats.say: There was a second thing. To stop yet another expensive war with the Native nations in the west, the King drew a line on the map along the mountains. The Royal Proclamation of 1763.
West of it, the land was reserved for Indigenous peoples. Colonists were told not to cross. From London, this looked like peace on the cheap.
Now the other side. The colonists had fought in that war too. Their men had died in it. And their reward was a new tax, and a wall of paper across the land they had hoped to settle.

scene.place: AND A LINE THEY MAY NOT CROSS

beats.say: And here's the part that really stung. They had no one in Parliament. Not one seat. People three thousand miles away were deciding what they paid, and they had no vote at all.
Both sides were right about something. That's what makes this story hard. London was right that someone had to pay. The colonists were right that someone should have asked them.
The first try was the Stamp Act of 1765. Newspapers, contracts, even playing cards would need a paid British stamp.
The colonies exploded. Boycotts, riots, tax collectors chased out of town. Within a year, Parliament backed down and repealed it.
Then it tried again, with new taxes on glass, paint, paper and tea. More boycotts. Most of those went too. All except one, kept on purpose, to prove a point. The tax on tea.

talk.text: Drop the taxes. All but tea.

beats.say: In Boston, troops and townspeople were now living on top of each other. In March 1770, a crowd threw snowballs and worse at a group of British soldiers. The soldiers fired. Five people died.

scene.caption: The Boston Massacre, by Paul Revere, 1770

beats.say: Patriots called it the Boston Massacre. And here's a detail most people don't know. The soldiers' defence lawyer at their trial was John Adams, a future President. Most of the soldiers walked free. Even the Revolution had people trying to be fair.

talk.text: John Adams is defending the soldiers?

beats.say: Now, the tea. In 1773, Parliament passed the Tea Act. And here's the irony. It made legal British tea cheaper, cheap enough to undercut the smugglers. Colonists would pay less for tea than before, as long as they accepted Parliament's right to tax it.

scene.place: CHEAPER TEA, IF YOU ACCEPT THE TAX

beats.say: They did not accept.

talk.text: Cheaper tea. And Parliament's right to tax it.

beats.say: On the night of the sixteenth of December 1773, men disguised as Mohawk warriors climbed aboard the ships, and dumped three hundred and forty two chests of tea into Boston Harbor. About ten thousand pounds' worth.

rows: Chests of tea in the harbour

beats.say: Ten thousand pounds, over three hundred and forty two chests. About twenty nine pounds a chest. Nearly what London paid to keep one soldier in America for a year. Every chest.
The most expensive tea party in history, thrown over tea that had just got cheaper.

From London, this wasn't a protest. It was a crime. Private property, destroyed by a mob. So Parliament punished Boston. It closed the harbour until the tea was paid for, and took control of the colony's government.

card.title: Boston Port Act, 1774
lines: until the tea is paid for.
until the tea is paid for.

talk.text: They threw it in the sea?
Close the harbour. Until it's paid for.

beats.say: London thought it was making an example of one city. Instead, it gave twelve other colonies a reason to stand next to it.
On the nineteenth of April 1775, British troops marched out of Boston to seize colonial weapons at Concord. At Lexington, someone fired. Nobody knows who. By the end of the day, the war had started.

Two months later, the rebels dug in on the hills above Boston. The plan was to fortify a place called Bunker Hill. They fortified the wrong hill. Most of the fighting happened on Breed's Hill, next door. History still calls it the Battle of Bunker Hill.
British troops marched straight up the slope, into the guns. Twice they were thrown back. On the third attack, the rebels ran out of gunpowder, and the British took the hill.

Britain won. And it was a disaster. More than a thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. The Americans lost about four hundred and fifty. A few more victories like that, and Britain would have no army left.
More than two British soldiers down, for every American.

And yet, even now, most colonists did not want independence. In July 1775, Congress sent the King one last letter. The Olive Branch Petition. It called the colonists his faithful subjects, and Britain their mother country. It begged him to help them make peace.

card.title: The Olive Branch Petition
lines: To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:
To the King's Most Excellent Majesty:

beats.say: Now the other side. To London, this was a letter from people who had just killed or wounded a thousand of the King's soldiers. The King refused it. He didn't even look at it. His answer, months later, declared the colonies in open rebellion.

talk.text: A petition from the colonies, Your Majesty.

beats.say: It was the last chance to stop the war with words. Both sides were too angry, too proud, or too far away to take it.

Now rewind a little, because here's where the Franklins come in. In 1774, Benjamin Franklin wasn't a revolutionary. He was in London, the colonies' man at court, still trying to keep the empire together. He was famous, admired, and proud to be British.
Here is how it went wrong. In December 1772, Franklin gets hold of about twenty private letters, written by the men who run Massachusetts, among them Thomas Hutchinson.

lines: "...an abridgement of what are called English liberties..."

beats.say: He sends them to Boston, with one condition. Do not publish them. By June 1773, they are in a Boston newspaper.

talk.text: Then why is it on my front page?

beats.say: Crowds burn the governor in effigy on Boston Common. And in London, two men fight a duel over who leaked the letters.
So on Christmas Day 1773, Franklin publishes a letter admitting that he sent them, to stop a second duel.
Then, in front of the King's Privy Council, he was publicly humiliated. He stood in silence while a government lawyer called him, more or less, a thief and a liar, in front of a laughing room.
That was the twenty ninth of January 1774. The lawyer was the Solicitor General, Alexander Wedderburn. Soon after, Franklin was fired from his post as Postmaster General.
He went home to America. He did not come back a loyal Briton.

His son William had taken a different road. Since 1763 he had been the Royal Governor of New Jersey, appointed by the Crown. In January 1775, he stood up in front of the New Jersey assembly, and urged it to stay loyal to King George.

scene.caption: William Franklin, Royal Governor of New Jersey

beats.say: His father expected him to resign in protest. William's advice to his father, in short: take your medicine, and retire.
His Two Roads speech asked New Jersey to choose loyalty over civil war. The assembly answered by voting, unanimously, to support Boston.
One Franklin was becoming a rebel. The other was the King's man. Same family, same dinner table, opposite sides of the line.
A year later, on the fourth of July 1776, the colonies declared independence. Benjamin Franklin helped edit the Declaration, and signed it.
By then, his son had already been arrested.

talk.text: William Franklin. You are under arrest.

beats.say: William Franklin was removed from office and held prisoner. After the rebels found he was still helping the Loyalist cause, he was put in solitary confinement in Litchfield, Connecticut, for eight months.
While he was there, his wife was dying. He asked for permission to see her. It was refused. She died while he was still in his cell.

talk.text: Let me see my wife. Please.

beats.say: His father was in France by then, working on the deal that would decide the whole war.
And with him went a sixteen year old secretary. Temple Franklin. William's own son, raised by his grandfather.

From William's side, he had kept an oath to his King. From Benjamin's side, his son had chosen a tyrant over his own people. That was the American Revolution in one family. And thousands of families split exactly the same way.
Britain had a problem. It had the best navy in the world, and a fairly small army, spread across a whole empire. So it did what European powers did all the time back then. It rented one.

Six German states signed contracts with King George. Their princes got paid, and their soldiers got shipped across the ocean. About thirty thousand men in total. More than half came from Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Hanau, so the Americans called all of them Hessians.

talk.text: You hired foreign soldiers to fight us?

beats.say: To London, this was ordinary. To the colonists, it was proof the King saw them as enemies, not subjects. Hiring foreign soldiers made it into the Declaration of Independence, as one of the complaints against him.

lines: He is at this time transporting

beats.say: And now, the most famous night of the war. By Christmas 1776, the Revolution was losing badly. Washington's army had been chased out of New York, and was shrinking by the day.
On the night after Christmas, he crossed the icy Delaware River, and hit the Hessian garrison at Trenton by surprise. Nearly a thousand of them were captured.

talk.text: Only the river. Nobody attacks at Christmas.

beats.say: It wasn't a big battle. But it told everyone the rebellion was still alive.
For the Germans, this was a war that had nothing to do with them. Roughly a quarter of them never went home. About seven and a half thousand died, most of them from disease, not bullets.

talk.text: Remind me why we are here?

beats.say: And between five and six thousand chose to stay. Many settled in British Canada. Others joined German communities in Pennsylvania and nearby, and became Americans, in the country they had been sent to stop.
In October 1777, a whole British army marching down from Canada was trapped, and forced to surrender at Saratoga.

scene.caption: The Surrender of General Burgoyne at Saratoga, 1777

beats.say: In Paris, Benjamin Franklin had been waiting for exactly this.

France had lost Canada to Britain only fifteen years earlier. It had been looking for revenge ever since. Saratoga proved the Americans could actually win. So in early 1778, France signed an alliance with the United States.
Spain joined the war the next year. Then the Dutch. And here is the dark joke of the whole story.

Britain had started taxing the colonies to pay for its last war against France. Now it was fighting France again. And Spain. And the Dutch. On almost every ocean at once. The bill it had tried to send to America was getting bigger by the month.

talk.text: France, Spain and the Dutch, sir.

beats.say: Inside America, this wasn't one people against a king. It was closer to a civil war. Loyalists and Patriots burned each other's farms. Neighbours turned in neighbours.
And for some people, the choice of side was about freedom, in the most literal sense.
In 1775, the British governor of Virginia, Lord Dunmore, promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped from rebel masters and joined the British.

lines: able and willing to bear arms…

talk.text: Is it true? Freedom, if we reach the British?

beats.say: Over the war, British offers like that freed about twenty thousand people. Black soldiers fought on the American side too. Both armies talked about liberty. Only one of them was offering it to the people the other side held in chains, and even that offer was made to win a war, not to end slavery.

lines: able and willing to bear arms…

beats.say: And many of the Native nations of the west fought alongside Britain, for a simple reason. The Proclamation Line of 1763 was the only thing protecting their land from the settlers. If the Americans won, that line would disappear.

scene.place: THE ONLY LINE PROTECTING THEIR LAND

beats.say: By 1781, the British commander in the south, Lord Cornwallis, had marched his army to Yorktown, on the coast of Virginia. The plan was simple. Sit by the sea, and let the Royal Navy bring supplies, or carry the army away.
The Royal Navy never came. A French fleet got there first, fought the British ships off the coast, and closed the door.
On land, American and French armies dug in around the town, and started shelling it, day and night.
On the nineteenth of October 1781, Cornwallis surrendered his entire army.
Legend says the British band played a song called The World Turned Upside Down, as they marched out. Nobody can prove it. But it's hard to think of a better soundtrack.

The news took more than a month to cross the Atlantic. It reached London on the twenty fifth of November. The Prime Minister, Lord North, had spent the whole war insisting it could still be won. When he heard, he is said to have cried out.
Thirty seven days, from Yorktown to London.

talk.text: Oh God. It is all over.

beats.say: Four months later, he resigned. From London, it wasn't only a defeat. It was the end of an idea, that the empire could be one people, under one Parliament, on both sides of an ocean.
Back to William. In 1778, he walks out of prison in a prisoner exchange, and goes straight to New York, held by the British.
There, he becomes the leader of the Loyalists. He builds a network of spies, and raises Loyalist fighting units.
He wants a guerrilla war against the rebels. The British commander, General Henry Clinton, has little use for the idea, or for Loyalists.
But by 1780, William has official blessing. A group called the Associated Loyalists starts raiding New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.
In New Jersey, neighbours are now killing neighbours, and every killing gets an answer.
In March 1782, a Loyalist named Philip White is killed by Patriot militiamen. Accounts differ. One says he was shot trying to escape. Another says he was executed.
On the twelfth of April, Loyalists take a Patriot militia captain, Joshua Huddy, and hang him by the shore. Huddy was not even there when White was killed.
On his body, they leave a note.
The men who did it belonged to William Franklin's Associated Loyalists. One account says he signed the order himself. Historians still argue how much he knew.
Washington demands the officer who led the hanging, Richard Lippincott. A British court martial tries him, and lets him go.
So Washington decides that someone else will pay. A British officer, of the same rank as Huddy, chosen by lot.

The twenty seventh of May 1782. The Black Bear Tavern, in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The names of captured British officers are drawn. A drummer boy pulls out one name, and with it, a paper marked Unfortunate.
Charles Asgill is a young captain, captured at Yorktown. And that is the problem. The Yorktown surrender, which Washington himself signed, protects him from exactly this.
Washington writes that the choice has distressed him exceedingly. But the order stands.
In England, Asgill's mother hears the news. Lady Asgill writes to the court of France, begging for her son's life.
And here is the strangest turn of the whole war. King Louis the Sixteenth and Queen Marie Antoinette, at war with Britain, ask Washington to spare a British officer.
Their foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, writes to Washington on the twenty ninth of July.
The French letter is read out in Congress on the very day it was planning to vote on hanging him.

talk.text: A letter. From the King of France.

beats.say: On the seventh of November 1782, after days of debate, Congress lets him go.
A hundred and sixty four days, from the paper marked Unfortunate, to freedom.

scene.place: WAITING TO LEARN IF HE WOULD HANG

beats.say: He rides for New York, misses his ship, pays a crew to row him out to catch it, and reaches England on the eighteenth of December.
At home, he hides in the bulrushes at the end of the garden, and sends the ship's captain in first with a letter, so the shock won't hurt his parents.

talk.text: A letter, my lady. Good news.
She won't come down. She thinks it's bad news.

beats.say: The whole affair stalled the peace talks in Paris. And sitting at those talks, for the Americans, was Benjamin Franklin. A crisis his son's men had started, landing on his father's table.
By then, William had already sailed for Britain. He left America in 1782, and never came back.
On the third of September 1783, Britain signed the Treaty of Paris, and recognised the United States. And once again, men drew a line on a map.

scene.caption: The Treaty of Paris (Benjamin West, unfinished)

beats.say: The new border ran through the middle of the Great Lakes, west to a place called the Lake of the Woods, and then down the Mississippi River.

talk.text: Through the middle of the Great Lakes.

beats.say: There was one small problem. The negotiators thought the Mississippi started up there. It doesn't. That mistake, fixed with more lines later, is part of the reason a small piece of Minnesota is still cut off from the rest of the United States today.
The old Proclamation Line was gone. The Native nations who had fought beside Britain weren't even invited to the talks. Britain simply handed over land it had promised to protect.

And the losers had to leave. About sixty thousand Loyalists left the new United States, taking about fifteen thousand enslaved people with them. Many went north, into what is now Canada. Others went to Jamaica and the Bahamas.
Sixty thousand Loyalists, and fifteen thousand enslaved people taken with them. Seventy five thousand people, leaving one country for another.
Some of the Black Loyalists, who had been promised freedom, went on to Africa. In 1791, they founded Freetown, in Sierra Leone.

Around twenty five thousand Americans died in the Revolution. Only about seven thousand of them in battle. Many of the rest died of disease as prisoners. Around seven and a half thousand German soldiers died. And many thousands of British soldiers never came home.
Fewer than one in three of them died in battle.
And the Franklins? At the peace talks, Benjamin refused to let the British win any compensation for the Loyalists. His son was one of them.
His grandson Temple, the secretary at those same talks, quietly asked one of the British negotiators if something could be done for his father.
In London, the British government paid William one thousand eight hundred pounds. That was the value of his furniture. Nothing for his lands. Plus a pension of eight hundred pounds a year.
Eight hundred pounds a year. About what it once cost to keep twenty six British soldiers in America.
On the twenty second of July 1784, William wrote to his father, hoping to make peace. The answer came three weeks later. Polite. Careful.

lines: I hope we may be reconciled…

beats._orig: William wrote to his father in 1784, hoping to make peace. He got a cold reply. They met once more, a year later, briefly, to talk about money.

beats.say: His father wrote back that they would try, as William proposed, to forget what had happened, as well as they could.

lines: mutually to forget what has happened
relating to it, as well we can."

beats.say: They met once more, in England, in 1785. Briefly. To tie up money and land.
That same winter, in January 1785, a letter from William to his son Temple crossed the English Channel in a hydrogen balloon. The first airmail in history.
In his will of 1788, Benjamin left his son some land in Nova Scotia that was worth almost nothing. And he wrote down why.
beats._orig: In his will, Benjamin left his son some land in Nova Scotia that was worth almost nothing. His reasoning, more or less: if the British had won, there would have been nothing to leave anyone.

beats.say: The part he acted against me in the late war, which is of public notoriety, will account for my leaving him no more of an estate he endeavoured to deprive me of.

lines: "The part he acted against me in the late war,
which is of public notoriety, will account for
my leaving him no more of an estate
he endeavoured to deprive me of."

beats.say: William Franklin died in London in 1813. Today, nobody knows exactly where his grave is.

Today, this is the longest border between two countries anywhere in the world. On one side, a country built by the people who won. On the other, a country built partly by the people who lost, and who refused to stop being British.
Two neighbours. Two very different memories of the same war.

outro.text: Every border has two sides. And this one began with a father and a son who never forgave each other.
outro.question: Would you have been a Patriot or a Loyalist?

hook: In 1763, Britain won the biggest war the world had ever seen. Twenty years later, it had lost America.
about: The American Revolution (1775–1783), told from both sides: the war debt that started it, the Stamp Act and the Boston Tea Party, Bunker Hill, Benjamin Franklin and his Loyalist son William, the 30,000 German soldiers Britain hired, Yorktown, and the Treaty of Paris that drew the border between the United States and Canada.

de.title: Wie Großbritannien Amerika verlor: Die Amerikanische Revolution von beiden Seiten
de.description:
1763 gewann Großbritannien den größten Krieg, den die Welt je gesehen hatte. Zwanzig Jahre später hatte es Amerika verloren.

Die Amerikanische Revolution (1775–1783), erzählt von beiden Seiten: die Kriegsschulden, die alles auslösten, die Boston Tea Party, Bunker Hill, Benjamin Franklin und sein königstreuer Sohn William, die 30.000 deutschen Soldaten, die Großbritannien anheuerte, Yorktown und der Frieden von Paris, der die Grenze zwischen den USA und Kanada zog.

es.title: Cómo Gran Bretaña perdió América: la Revolución Americana desde ambos lados
es.description:
En 1763, Gran Bretaña ganó la guerra más grande que el mundo había visto. Veinte años después, había perdido América.

La Revolución Americana (1775–1783) contada desde ambos lados: la deuda de guerra que lo empezó todo, el Motín del Té de Boston, Bunker Hill, Benjamin Franklin y su hijo leal a la Corona, William, los 30.000 soldados alemanes contratados por Gran Bretaña, Yorktown y el Tratado de París que trazó la frontera entre Estados Unidos y Canadá.

fr.title: Comment la Grande-Bretagne a perdu l'Amérique : la Révolution américaine des deux côtés
fr.description:
En 1763, la Grande-Bretagne a gagné la plus grande guerre que le monde ait connue. Vingt ans plus tard, elle avait perdu l'Amérique.

La Révolution américaine (1775–1783) racontée des deux côtés : la dette de guerre à l'origine de tout, la Boston Tea Party, Bunker Hill, Benjamin Franklin et son fils loyaliste William, les 30 000 soldats allemands engagés par la Grande-Bretagne, Yorktown et le traité de Paris qui a tracé la frontière entre les États-Unis et le Canada.

pt.title: Como a Grã-Bretanha perdeu a América: a Revolução Americana dos dois lados
pt.description:
Em 1763, a Grã-Bretanha venceu a maior guerra que o mundo já tinha visto. Vinte anos depois, tinha perdido a América.

A Revolução Americana (1775–1783) contada dos dois lados: a dívida de guerra que começou tudo, a Festa do Chá de Boston, Bunker Hill, Benjamin Franklin e seu filho legalista William, os 30.000 soldados alemães contratados pela Grã-Bretanha, Yorktown e o Tratado de Paris que traçou a fronteira entre os Estados Unidos e o Canadá.
